title: Reading one line of his
hook: pick one line of the Tenth Guru and live with it for a day

segments.voice: Yesterday, sword and pen: the saint-soldier, with doing good written first. Your line was pen and sword. Which line of your little poem stayed with you? Day one thousand two hundred fifty.

A tune heard once at breakfast can still be playing in your head at dinner. Nobody learned it on purpose. It was short enough to stay, and by evening it has been everywhere you went. Sikh life has a version of this. In a gurdwara, the morning's hukamnama, one hymn read from the Guru Granth Sahib, is carried home by some Sikhs as the word for the day. Today we try that with the Tenth Guru. Not his whole book. One line.
screen: `A TUNE THAT STAYS ALL DAY.` → `THE WORD FOR THE DAY.` → `NOT THE WHOLE BOOK. ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: Here are three lines from his writings we've met along the way, each paraphrased. Pick the one that catches. The first is from the Akal Ustat: recognize the whole human race as one. That's a line for a crowded train, a line for the person you'd rather not sit next to. Live with it for a day and every face becomes a test of it. The second comes from the morning swayyas, which sit in the same work. In paraphrase, the Guru says: I tell you the truth, all of you, listen: only those who have loved have found the Lord. That's a line about the heart under the ritual. Live with it for a day and you start asking where love actually went in what you did. The third is from the Bachitar Natak, about himself. Whoever calls me God, he warns, will fall; I am only the servant of the Supreme. That's a line about humility, from someone with every reason to be proud. Live with it for a day and watch how often you'd like a little credit. Why only one? Because a line has to be carried to be read. Read a whole page and it stays on the page. Carry one line and it starts reading you back. It shows up at the sink, in a meeting, in a mood. That fits a habit in Sikh life: the word is not finished when the book closes. One line, one day, is enough to find out what the Tenth Guru's words do when they leave the page.
screen: `ONE HUMAN RACE: A LINE FOR CROWDS.` · `ONLY THOSE WHO LOVED FOUND THE LORD.` · `ONLY THE SERVANT: A LINE FOR PRIDE.` · `CARRY ONE, AND IT READS YOU BACK.` · then, large: `ONE LINE, ONE DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose your line. Settle, and breathe. Let the three pass by again: one human race; only those who loved; only the servant. Don't pick the one you think is best. Pick the one that pricks a little. Then say it slowly in your head, matching it to your breath, half on the in-breath, half on the out. Keep returning to it until the bell. If you pray, you can let it rest beside the name Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Reading one line of his. Choosing a single line of Guru Gobind Singh's writings and carrying it through a whole day, so the words leave the page. Today's word.
screen: `READING ONE LINE OF HIS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: one line, one day. Today, write the line you chose on something you'll see three times: a mirror, a wrist, a phone screen. Day one thousand two hundred fifty.

screen: `DAY 1250 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TENTH GURU'S WRITINGS CLOSE.`

howItsDone: Some Sikhs carry the morning hukamnama from the gurdwara as the word for the day, and some take a line from the Nitnem, including the Tenth Guru's compositions, to recall through the day.

only those who loved found the Lord

myth: the way to read his writings is to read the whole book at once
today's way is one line, carried for a day, so it leaves the page.
in the Bachitar Natak, the Guru warns against calling him God
whoever calls him God will fall, he says; he is only the servant of the Supreme.
the swayyas line says ritual is how the Lord is found
it says only those who have loved have found the Lord.

fork.setup: you've read three lines of the Tenth Guru. which should you carry through today?
options: the one that pricks a little.
the one that sounds best out loud.
fork.reveal: one line, the one that catches, carried long enough that it starts reading you back.

trapdoor: what you thought: reading means getting through the book.
what it means: one line, carried for a day, until it shows up in your choices.
what a scholar hears: the same habit as the daily hukamnama, a word for the day, turned toward the Tenth Guru's compositions.
recall: ten hymns of Guru Gobind Singh

sources.ref: Akal Ustat 85 (Dasam Granth): recognize all humankind as one, paraphrased
Tav Prasad Swayye (Akal Ustat): only those who have loved have found the Lord, paraphrased
Bachitar Natak 6 (Dasam Granth): whoever calls me God will fall; I am the servant, paraphrased

notes: All three lines are paraphrased; please check the paraphrases and the references (Akal Ustat 85; 'sach kahon sun leho sabhai, jin prem kio tin hi prabh paio' in the Tav Prasad Swayye; Bachitar Natak 6).
The Bachitar Natak line says those who call him God will fall into hell; the script softens it to 'will fall'. Please confirm this is acceptable.
'Some Sikhs carry the morning hukamnama home as the word for the day' is a general description; please confirm or soften.

Editor: replaced the sticky-note-on-the-mirror hook (too close to day 1242's list on the fridge) with a tune that stays all day; softened 'Sikhs know this way of reading well'; named the morning swayyas so they are not confused with the thirty-three.
